# Release readiness: TestFlight, App Store, Google Play

What has to be true before a Scribl build reaches a tester, and later a store.
Split into prerequisites, things that live in this repo, and things that live in
a console.

---

## 1. Prerequisites

Required before the corresponding activity can start. Scribl provides the
production accounts; Bounteous configures and operates them.

| Prerequisite | Needed before | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Apple Developer Program membership, active | Any signed build, any physical device install, TestFlight, App Store | Nothing in sections 4 or 5 starts without it. Simulator development does not need it |
| Signing certificate and provisioning profile under that membership | Any signed build | Distribution profile for TestFlight and App Store |
| App Store Connect app record, bundle id `co.scribl.app` registered | First upload | The identifier is fixed from the first upload onward |
| App Store Connect API key | Automated or scripted upload | Prefer this over a shared Apple ID. It is revocable, scoped, and does not break when someone changes a password or takes leave |
| Google Play Developer account | Android internal track and Play release | Lower urgency while Android is a fast follow |
| Play App Signing enrolment and an upload key | First Android upload | Key held in the pipeline secret store |
| AWS account | Any deploy, any hosted environment | One account confirmed. Local development needs no credential, by design |
| A domain plus small static hosting | Deep linking, the store-required legal pages, and Play's deletion path | See section 2. This is a hard requirement for a store release, not a nice-to-have |
| Privacy policy and terms content | The in-app consent surface and both stores | Content is a client and legal deliverable, not an engineering one |

Simulator development, the local API, the full test suite and infrastructure
synthesis all work with none of the above. That is deliberate. Nobody waits.

---

## 2. Hosted web surfaces

Four surfaces are needed. They can be one small static site plus one API
endpoint, so provision the domain and hosting once rather than four times.

| Surface | Required by |
|---|---|
| Privacy policy, publicly reachable | Apple metadata, Play metadata, and the in-app consent screen |
| Terms of service, publicly reachable | Consent surface, store metadata |
| Account deletion request page | **Google Play requires a web-accessible deletion path** in addition to in-app deletion. A thin client over the deletion endpoint the app already exposes |
| Universal-link and app-link association files | Deep linking on both platforms. Must be served from the domain itself, with no redirect |

The invite landing page in the client's designed flow, if it is in scope, is an
additional page on the same site rather than a separate piece of work. Whether
that flow is in scope this phase is tracked in `code-questions.md`.

## 3. In-repo build artifacts

Built by the scaffold, deliverable 8. Listed here so the release owner verifies
rather than rediscovers.

**Status as of 2026-08-31**, against the frontend scaffold on branch
`architect/frontend_base_setup`. "Built" means the artifact exists and was
observed in a generated native project, not merely that it was intended.

| Artifact | Platform | Status | Why, and where it lives |
|---|---|---|---|
| Privacy manifest | iOS | **Built** | Declared in `app.config.ts` under `ios.privacyManifests` and generated into the Xcode project by prebuild, rather than committed as a second file that could drift from it. Declares crash and other-diagnostic data, not linked to identity and not used for tracking; `NSPrivacyTracking` false with no tracking domains. **The required-reason codes must be verified against Apple's current list before a submission**, not trusted from the repo. Third-party SDKs on Apple's list must ship their own signed manifests, **so audit every dependency before adding it**, Firebase included |
| Permission purpose strings | iOS | **Built** | `NSFaceIDUsageDescription` only. No microphone string while voice is out of scope, and no camera, location or tracking strings at all. Verified in the generated `Info.plist`: Face ID is the single entry |
| Deployment target | iOS | **Built, number resolved: 16.4** | This is Expo SDK 57's own enforced minimum, read from `expo-build-properties` (which rejects anything lower). React Native 0.86.3's floor is 15.1, from `react-native/scripts/cocoapods/helpers.rb`, and an iPhone 11 runs well past both, so the Expo floor is the binding number. **Re-read both files on every SDK upgrade.** Note this is SDK 57, not the 56 the scaffold assumed |
| App Transport Security at secure default | iOS | **Built** | No arbitrary loads and no per-domain exceptions are declared |
| Export compliance declaration | iOS | **Built** | `ITSAppUsesNonExemptEncryption` false, set in the Info.plist so uploads do not stop to ask. Standard TLS and the platform keystore only. Confirm the claim still holds if anything cryptographic is added |
| Monotonic build number from the pipeline | Both | **Built** | Derived from the CI run number in `scripts/build-ios.sh` and the iOS release workflow. Never generated by hand |
| Debug symbols retained and uploaded to Crashlytics | Both | **Not built** | Blocked with Crashlytics itself, see section 7 |
| Firebase config files committed, config plugin wired | Both | **Not built** | Blocked on the privacy-manifest audit and the Kids Category question. The location is decided: `assets/firebase/`, committed, **not** `ios/` or `android/`, because those are generated by prebuild and gitignored, and git does not descend into an ignored directory |
| App bundle output, not APK | Android | **Built** | `scripts/build-android.sh` produces a bundle for release and keeps a debug APK path for internal testing |
| Target and compile SDK at current Play requirement | Both | **Built, number resolved: 36** | Compile and target SDK 36, min SDK 24, from the Expo SDK 57 defaults. Play enforces a rolling minimum with published deadlines. Track the next one |
| Runtime notification permission, scoped media access | Android | **Built** | The production manifest declares exactly `INTERNET`, `POST_NOTIFICATIONS`, `USE_BIOMETRIC`, `USE_FINGERPRINT` and `VIBRATE`. Camera, microphone, location and both legacy storage permissions are explicitly blocked, as is `SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW`, which the Expo template otherwise leaves in the main manifest and which would ship as an unused permission |
| Upload key in the pipeline secret store | Android | **Not built** | Needs the Play account. The build script stops after prebuild when the key is absent, which is the correct behaviour until then |
| Seeded reviewer demo account | Both | **Not built** | Backend-owned. See the demo-account trap in section 4; the contract mock reproduces the shape so the client path is exercisable |

## 4. TestFlight

Distribution is TestFlight, sized at **100 testers or fewer**. That cap matters
more than it looks, because it puts internal distribution within reach and
internal distribution skips review entirely.

| | Internal testers | External testers |
|---|---|---|
| Cap | 100 | 10,000 |
| Review | **None.** Build is available as soon as it finishes processing | **Beta App Review required** |
| Turnaround | Minutes | Typically a day or two, slowest on the first submission of a version |
| What a tester needs | An App Store Connect user account on the team | Just an email address or a public link |

**The recommendation, given 100 or fewer: use internal testing.** No beta review
means a build reaches a tester in minutes, which takes review turnaround off the
critical path before every demo. The trade is that each internal tester must be
an App Store Connect user on the team, which is fine for the delivery team and
the client's core stakeholders, and awkward if testers are wider than that.

If testers turn out to be wider than the account can reasonably hold, the
fallback is external testing, and then Beta App Review needs all of:

- A beta app description of what to test
- A feedback email address
- A publicly reachable privacy policy URL
- **Working demo credentials, because the app is sign-in gated**
- A build that does not crash on launch

**The demo-account trap, which applies to both paths and to App Store review.**
Submit-to-unlock means a fresh account sees an empty wall. A reviewer given clean
credentials cannot evaluate the product and will reject the build as incomplete.
The demo account must arrive **pre-seeded** with a submission and visible wall
content. The scaffold automates that seeding behind a documented flag. Do not
hand-build it the night before a submission.

Operational facts worth knowing: builds expire 90 days after upload, so a build
cut early in a sprint can lapse before it is used. Every upload needs its own
build number. Whatever path is chosen, the planning consequence is that the first
signed build and first upload is realistically a day of work end to end, and
that day is only enough if the prerequisites in section 1 are already closed.

## 5. Apple App Store review, the requirements this app actually triggers

| Guideline | Requirement | Where it is handled |
|---|---|---|
| 1.2 User-generated content | Filtering objectionable material, reporting content, **blocking abusive users**, a published contact route, and prompt action on reports | Deliverable 7: reports table, block relationship enforced in the authorization choke point, named-owner and SLA fields. Automated filtering is a later epic, so the human path must be complete |
| 2.1 App completeness | A functioning build and **demo credentials for a sign-in-gated app** | Seeded reviewer account, deliverable 8. See the demo-account trap above |
| 2.3 Accurate metadata | Screenshots and description match the shipped app | Release process, after the UI settles |
| 4.5.4 Push notifications | Push must not be required to use the app, and must be opt-out | Managed push is out of scope this phase. The local reminder is on-device and opt-out by permission |
| 4.8 Login services | If a third-party social login is offered, an equivalent privacy-preserving option must be too | **Not triggered.** Auth is email and password only. Adding Google or Facebook sign-in later triggers this; treat it as a product decision, not a small feature |
| 5.1.1 Data collection | Privacy policy, purpose strings, data minimisation, **in-app account deletion** | Deliverables 3, 7 and 8 |
| 5.1.2(i) Data use and sharing | Consent before sharing content with a third party, no training use without opt-in | Deliverable 7. The `third_party_ai` consent kind, default off, and the text-only model boundary |
| 5.1.4 Kids and COPPA | Stricter data, advertising and consent rules for children | **In scope.** Under-13 users are a supported audience, so this applies rather than being avoided. Verifiable parental consent, stricter retention and a stricter moderation posture all become requirements. [ADR-0012](/context/pages/reference/decisions/0012-coppa-under-13-support) records the age-gate mechanism already shipped; production still declines to enrol minors until store-category targeting and the verifiable-consent method close. See section 9 |
| App Privacy label | Nutrition-label declaration in App Store Connect | Console metadata. **Must be consistent with the privacy manifest in the repo**, and with what Crashlytics actually collects, or the mismatch surfaces at review |
| Age rating questionnaire | Answered honestly. User-generated content raises the floor | Console metadata, and the answer interacts with the COPPA position |

Also required in metadata and easy to forget: a support URL, a marketing URL and
a copyright line.

**Two release-phase assignments, not engineering work.** Guideline 1.2 expects a
named person who acts on reported content within a committed turnaround. The
schema carries the owner and SLA fields; the assignment itself is a decision to
make before submission, not before development. Same for who answers the age
rating questionnaire.

## 6. Google Play review

Android is a fast follow, so this is preparation. Two items are structural and
are already in the scaffold.

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **Data Safety form** | Mandatory declaration, analogous to Apple's label. Must match actual behaviour, Crashlytics included |
| **Web account-deletion path** | Structural. Distinct from Apple, commonly missed, covered in section 2 |
| Target API level | Rolling minimum with published deadlines. Track the next one |
| Families policy | Applies if the listing targets children. Interacts with the COPPA position |
| UGC policy | Report and block mechanisms, same substrate as Apple 1.2 |
| Sensitive permission declarations | Justification forms for anything sensitive. Keep the permission set minimal |
| Privacy policy URL, content rating questionnaire | Console metadata |
| App bundle, Play App Signing | Structural, deliverable 8 |

## 7. Crash reporting and what it means for both stores

Firebase Crashlytics on the free tier, and it has declaration consequences on
both platforms.

**Current state, 2026-08-31: the seam is complete and the vendor is not wired.**
`services/crash/` has the interface, a local adapter that is genuinely useful in
development, a Crashlytics adapter written against an injected bridge, a factory,
and a conformance suite run against both. What is absent is
`@react-native-firebase/crashlytics` itself, deliberately, for three reasons:

1. It is a native module and does nothing until `expo prebuild` runs against a
   real Firebase project. No Firebase project exists yet.
2. Every dependency must be audited for its own Apple privacy manifest **before**
   it is added, Firebase included, with the outcome recorded in the ADR. That
   audit has not been done.
3. If the Kids Category question resolves toward that category, the third-party
   SDK rules tighten and this choice may have to be revisited. Linking it in now
   risks work on a compliance path nobody has chosen.

Selecting `EXPO_PUBLIC_CRASH_ADAPTER=crashlytics` today throws with that
explanation rather than silently reporting nothing.

**To finish it, in order:** create the Firebase project; audit the Firebase SDK
versions for signed privacy manifests and record the result in the ADR; commit
the two config files to `assets/firebase/`; add the package and its config
plugin; supply the real bridge to the existing adapter; add the debug-symbol
upload step to the iOS release workflow; and confirm Firebase Analytics is not
initialised, since it ships inside the same pods and is explicitly out of scope.
Nothing above the adapter changes.

- Crashlytics collects crash traces plus an installation identifier. That is
  data collection, and it appears in the App Privacy label and the Play Data
  Safety form. Declare it; do not leave it out because it is diagnostic.
- Firebase SDKs must carry their own signed privacy manifests for the iOS
  requirement. **Audit this at the version being added**, and record the result
  in the crash-reporting ADR.
- **Collection starts disabled and is enabled after consent.** The scaffold wires
  the toggle. This matters more if the COPPA position lands on under-13 in scope,
  where diagnostic collection on a child's device without consent is a policy
  problem on both stores.
- Firebase Analytics is deliberately **not** in scope. Adding it changes both
  declarations and is a product decision rather than a technical one.

---

## 9. Under-13 in scope, and what it changes here

Under-13 users are a supported audience. That decision reaches further into the
release path than any other on this page, so it gets its own section.

**The Kids Category question comes first.** An app can serve under-13 users
either inside Apple's Kids Category or outside it, and they are different
regimes. Inside, the placement is a marketing advantage and the rules tighten
considerably: restrictions on third-party analytics and advertising SDKs, on
external links, and on anything that takes a child out of the app without a
parental gate. Outside, COPPA still applies as law and the age rating must reflect
the audience, but the SDK rules are the ordinary ones. **This has to be answered
before the listing is built and before the SDK set is final**, because it can
retroactively disqualify a dependency. It is one of the two open sub-decisions
in [ADR-0012](/context/pages/reference/decisions/0012-coppa-under-13-support).

**Consequences on this page:**

| Area | What changes |
|---|---|
| Age rating | Answered against the under-13 audience, not defaulted. Interacts with the user-generated-content floor from guideline 1.2 |
| Verifiable parental consent | Required before a minor's account is usable. COPPA's approved methods vary enormously in cost; ADR-0012 names the options but does not pick one yet. Production does not enrol minors until it does |
| Crashlytics | Diagnostic collection on a minor's device needs parental consent, so the consent gate must hold and be tested. **May need revisiting entirely if we target the Kids Category** |
| Speech-to-text, if voice lands | Sending a child's voice to a third-party service is a different data class from a typed sentence. Needs parental consent and, arguably, its own decision |
| App Privacy label and Play Data Safety | Both gain children's-data declarations. They must match the code, and a mismatch here is a worse finding than an omission |
| Play Families policy | Applies in parallel to Apple's rules, with its own declarations and its own SDK constraints |
| Moderation | Fail-safe stops being a product tradeoff and becomes a legal position for minor accounts |
| Retention | Tighter limits for minors, and deletion has to actually delete, including S3 objects |

**The honest planning note.** The project brain placed under-13 outside these
eight weeks, in the GRAY band, sized as "not sized," while separately listing the
COPPA position as one of four decisions blocking the build. Bringing it in scope
resolves the blocking decision and adds unsized work to a plan that was already
over capacity. It is the right call for a family drawing app, and it should be
sized and stated rather than absorbed quietly.

## 10. Producing a build, concretely

The commands live in the frontend repository and are committed as shell scripts
rather than inline pipeline YAML, so they can be run and tested on a developer's
own Mac exactly the way a hosted runner calls them. Full script surface is in
`toolchain.md` section 4; only the release-relevant ones are here.

| Step | Command | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Prove the gate | `npm run verify` | Mirrors the pull-request pipeline exactly. A green verify against a red pipeline means the two have drifted, which is a bug in the workflow file |
| Generate the native projects | `npm run prebuild:ios`, `npm run prebuild:android` | `ios/` and `android/` are generated and gitignored. Regenerating is a script, not a merge conflict |
| iOS build | `npm run build:ios:qa` or `:prod` | Runs prebuild, then archives and exports **only when `SCRIBL_SIGNING_CONFIGURED` is set**. Without it the script stops after prebuild, deliberately: no signed build is produced from a laptop |
| Android build | `npm run build:android:qa` or `:prod` | Produces a bundle when `SCRIBL_UPLOAD_KEYSTORE` is set, otherwise a debug APK |
| Upload | `npm run upload:ios` | Separate from the build on purpose, so a failed upload does not mean rebuilding. Needs the App Store Connect API key |

**Two host requirements that are not obvious and cost an afternoon each.**
CocoaPods needs a UTF-8 locale or `pod install` fails with a Ruby
`unicode_normalize` stack trace that names nothing relevant; export
`LANG=en_US.UTF-8`. And building for a simulator needs an iOS simulator runtime
installed through Xcode's Components pane, which is a multi-gigabyte download
separate from Xcode itself.

**Build variants.** Three environments with distinct identifiers, so a tester can
hold a QA build and a production build on one device without uninstalling the one
they are using: `co.scribl.app.dev`, `co.scribl.app.qa`, and the clean
`co.scribl.app` for production. Driven by `APP_ENV` through one dynamic config
function rather than three checked-in variants that drift.

## 11. Adapter selection in a release build

Every external dependency sits behind a seam whose adapter is chosen by a
build-time variable. **A production build refuses to start if any seam is still
on its local adapter**, which is the guard against the likeliest release mistake:
an omitted variable shipping an app that talks to nothing and looks fine.

| Seam | Release value | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `EXPO_PUBLIC_AUTH_ADAPTER` | `cognito` | Needs the pool id and app client id, which are **not secrets** and belong in the build. The mobile app client has no secret by design |
| `EXPO_PUBLIC_CRASH_ADAPTER` | `crashlytics` | Blocked, see section 7 |
| `EXPO_PUBLIC_LOGGING_ADAPTER` | `api` | Ships device logs to our own endpoint. Off by default and consent-gated regardless |
| `EXPO_PUBLIC_MEDIA_ADAPTER` | `s3` | Presigned PUT straight to S3; bytes never pass through the API |
| `EXPO_PUBLIC_NOTIFICATIONS_ADAPTER` | `sns` | Posts the device token to our API, which owns the SNS platform endpoint. See below |
| `EXPO_PUBLIC_FLAGS_ADAPTER` | `static` or `api` | `static` is a valid shipping configuration until `GET /flags` exists |

**Push, and why the device never talks to SNS.** Creating an SNS platform
endpoint is an authenticated AWS call. Doing it from the app would mean either a
credential in the binary, which is not a secret, or an unauthenticated identity
pool, which `service-seams.md` section 2 names as the signal that something is
putting credentials on an untrusted client. So the device gets its APNs or FCM
token from the OS and posts it to `POST /notifications/registrations`; the
backend creates the endpoint. Swapping SNS for another provider is then a backend
deploy rather than an App Store review, which is the whole point of the rule.

**Media, and the two halves.** Uploads are presigned: the client asks the API for
a presigned PUT and sends the bytes straight to S3, so the API never handles data
it does not need to see, and the content type and byte-size limits are enforced
in the presign rather than trusted from the client. Reads are the reverse: the
client never constructs a media URL, and the server returns short-TTL signed URLs
already authorized. The client media port has no URL-building method at all,
which is what keeps that true.

Both halves are exercisable before S3 exists: the contract mock issues presigns
against its own upload target, stores the bytes, and serves them back.

---

## 8. Sequence

What order to close things, for whoever owns the release path.

1. Confirm the section 1 prerequisites, Apple membership first. It gates the most.
2. Register the bundle id and create the App Store Connect record.
3. Stand up the domain and static hosting, and publish the privacy policy, terms
   and association files.
4. Land the section 3 build artifacts in the repo. They do not need an account.
5. Script the local signed build, then run it once all the way to TestFlight to
   prove the path end to end. Do this well before a demo depends on it.
6. Decide internal or external testing based on who the testers actually are.
7. Add testers, confirm the seeded demo account works from a clean install.
8. Store submission, when and if it is committed to.

Steps 4 and 5 are the ones that can start now. Everything else waits on step 1.
